title: Voice (sustained sung vowels)
reference_instrument: adult male voice, sustained vowels (VocalSet long tones, CC BY 4.0)
summary: Sustained vowels on C3, C4 and F4, with no words. The tract is another man's, from MRI of spoken German vowels, so the tilt follows the subject's vowels, not the singers'. Harmonics-to-noise is inside its ruler on 11 of 14 pages, but the shape is wrong even where the total is right. A vocal fold model self-oscillates against that tract (two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, with a tapered rest gap on C3-a, C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid, F4-e and F4-o, and Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold on F4-a), and the sound is read at a simulated microphone 0.30 m from the mouth, 45 degrees off axis, with a rigid sphere for the head and a larger one for the torso under it on the graded notes and the phrases. No source waveform or formant filter is applied. On the 14 graded notes the breath pressure acts at the far end of a branched airway below the folds, Weibel's symmetric tree with measured dimensions, whose walls carry the vocal-tract wall as a stand-in. One scale on the fold stiffnesses (Q on the body-cover fold) is the one model-only factor: trimmed on the model alone, it puts each card near its written note, so pitch isn't evidence. The graded notes are straight tones with a slow and a fast pitch row, a small cycle-to-cycle shimmer in the glottal pulse, and no vibrato. The phrases carry vibrato, with both pitch rows and the shimmer under it, and each vowel there is its own render, joined by crossfades. The /a/ at six pitches and the vowel ladder further down are older renders on earlier tracts.
physics_present: On the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, two-mass vocal folds on Ishizaka and Flanagan's 1972 law as printed, for the glottal flow and the forces on the masses, as a mirror pair, with masses and base stiffnesses from the licensed model-card pack. The oscillation isn't imposed: it comes from the fold, the flow, collision and the tract loop.

Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold (NCVS Status and Progress Report 6, 1994), case C of their Table 1, with that report's own pressure and flow law, on F4-a only. Q, one scale on its four stiffnesses, is the one model-only factor: trimmed to within 3 cents of the written note, it ended at 4.109 against a start of 4.633, then moved x 0.813 for the measured wall, to 3.340, and x 2.267 for the airway, to 7.572. Story and Titze's 0.8 kPa lung pressure isn't applied; the breath stays the card's player row. The fold misses its own paper's Table 2 on this model's test tube, and the paper's tube isn't printed. The other twelve pages it was tried on keep the two-mass fold: on the five C3 pages the measured tract holds its pitch off the note; on C4-a, C4-o, C4-u and F4-o its pitch jumps across the note between nearly equal values of Q; and C4-e, C4-i and F4-e reached their notes but didn't pass the posting rule. Re-tried on F4-e on the cards of 11-07, trimmed again to within 3 cents (Q 6.983), it moved the partial frequencies from 9.2 to 4.4 cents off the recording's and the period swing over the middle of the clip from 37.0 to 20.8 cents (5-95 %) against the recording's 19.8, and it raised the count from 5 to 6 of 14, but its harmonics-to-noise overshot the recording, 28.6 against 25.4 dB, a gap 1.06 dB wider, past the ruler's smallest value of 0.70, so it doesn't post. On the measured C3 tracts this fold's pitch stays at 125–157 Hz whatever its stiffness (Q 0.45–1.29); on a plain 17.5 cm tube the same fold at the same breath sings 108–114 Hz. The tract holds its pitch, so there are no C3 pages.

On C3-a, C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid, F4-e and F4-o, the two-mass fold takes the self-oscillating form of Birkholz, Kröger and Neuschaefer-Rube (2011): the masses move rigidly and the rest gap narrows to nothing at the front of the folds. The row has no number in it. On each of those pages the three fold stiffnesses were trimmed again for it, to within 3 cents of the written note, and both pitch rows were scaled once by the new gain. F4-o posted it on 2026-11-05 as an exception to that lane's posting rule; C3-a, C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid and F4-e posted it on 2026-11-08 by the count rule, a tie or a rise. On C3-i, C3-o, C4-e, C4-i and C4-o it was tried the same day and the count fell (C3-i 10 to 7, C3-o 14 to 11, C4-e 9 to 8, C4-i 15 to 14, C4-o 12 to 9), so those pages keep the uniform gap. F4-a's body-cover fold doesn't take the row.

A measured tract on every page: subject 1 of the Dresden Vocal Tract Dataset (Birkholz et al. 2020, CC0), a man in MRI of spoken German vowels, tense or lax by a rule fixed before any grade. The subject's tense /u/ on C3-u, C4-u and C4-u-rigid and in both phrases needs the glottal line's ceiling of 131072 taps, one doubling over the default, at the same tolerances. The cut from the subject's 3-D model to one dimension is this model's own (91 to 115 sections), and the dataset's own printed area functions aren't used.

Viscothermal loss and a flanged-piston mouth load from the transfer-matrix duct; on the 14 graded notes and the phrases the head_load row adds the change of the head, with the torso under it below 10 kHz, to that load, and the mouth flow and the passive formants read the same load.

A measured yielding wall on all 14 cards and on the phrases, including C4-u-rigid, whose name comes from an older comparison: per unit area 15.4 kg/m2, 3.79e5 Pa/m and 6.22e3 Pa s/m, from the wall inertance, tissue compliance and resistance Hanna, Smith and Wolfe (2016, Table III) measured in seven men through the lips with the glottis closed, in place of the Flanagan setting as given by Birkholz, Haesner and Kuerbis 2022 and its assumed stiffness. The wall alone took the notes 3.2 to 70.2 c off their pitch, so every card's folds are retrimmed to the note for it by the card's own rule: fold stiffness only, pressure held, within 3 c of the written note, no recording.

On the 14 graded notes and the phrases the tract holds alveolar air at 37 C, from the four partial pressures printed in OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4, Table 22.3, with the argon inside the nitrogen as printed. Outside the lips, and in the tracts of the older renders further down, the air is humid at body temperature. The medium is stationary and the lips' load stays the room's absolute impedance: the breath moved the tract's sound speed -1.19 %, and the passive first formants by -0.88 to -1.01 %, +0.18 to +0.31 % off that ratio; the wall and the losses don't scale with it either.

Sound at the microphone, 0.30 m away at 45 degrees off axis: on the 14 graded notes and the phrases, the mouth is a cap of the opening's area on a rigid sphere of radius 8.7 cm for the head, over a rigid sphere of radius 16.9 cm for the torso, 5.3 cm between their surfaces (the KEMAR snowman of Algazi, Duda and Thompson 2002, in place of the 8.75 cm head alone of Brown and Duda 1998; the head's field from Morse and Ingard's cap-on-sphere series), blended back to the infinite baffle over 8-10 kHz; the older renders further down still radiate through a baffled circular opening. The torso is a mannequin's: torso change checked against an independent boundary-element solve at 250, 600, 1200 and 2400 Hz (within 1.68 %); above that it rests on the model's own convergence. The pressure inside the tract is never the output. On the 14 graded notes and the phrases, each path from the mouth to the microphone also carries the absorption of the card's exterior air (the observer_law row): the oxygen and nitrogen vibrational relaxations of ISO 9613-1, with viscosity and heat conduction from the gas's own transport data; the head and torso still scatter without loss. Over 0.30 m it moves the served clips' 8 kHz third octave -0.015 to -0.010 dB re each clip's total, against -0.017 to -0.012 dB from ISO 9613-1 (13 pages; the grader started F4-o's cut 0.27 ms earlier, which moves its served clip more).

Slow pitch movement on the straight-tone notes and, under vibrato, on the phrases (Ternström and Friberg 1989 model; amplitude from choir singers told to sing straight), moving the fold stiffnesses (three on the two-mass cards, all four on the body-cover fold) and set for each two-mass card.

Fast pitch movement on the straight-tone notes, a second row in the same tension: the 18 to 33 Hz part of the movement Ternström and Friberg 1989 print for singers told to sing straight, 1.34 to 1.76 cents by vowel, read by eye from their Fig. 5, which is solid only to about 25 Hz and has no man at C4 or F4. It was sized once from each two-mass card's gain at 4 Hz and not iterated, so it reads 0.35 to 1.89 cents, the lowest on C4-u, and no recording enters. The recordings' fast movement looks like pitch at F4, but at C3 and C4 much of it doesn't, so part of what this row closes there may be noise in the recording.

Vibrato on the phrases only, with both pitch rows added under it on the same fold tension (adding them is a modelling choice; no print sets it): 5.9 Hz and +-69.5 cents, the means of 50 professional singers (Larrouy-Maestri, Magis and Morsomme 2014). The C4 phrase's tense /u/ swings +-260.9 cents on its render: the card's declared rescale doubles the depth at the halved tension-to-pitch gain, and near the tract's first resonance (264.4 Hz) the swing does not stay linear.

On the 14 graded notes and the phrases the glottal jet's noise comes from a measured duct-constriction law (the constriction_noise row: Oldham and Ukpoho 1990, K(St) measured on dampers and orifice plates, extrapolated to the glottis; no gain and no gate, its one number the radius of the first tract section), in place of the Verge 1995 flue-jet row. It is a substitution: both rows would count the jet twice. The jet row's gate was a flow threshold: on the graded notes it sounded for part of each note at C4 and F4, only briefly at C3, and not at all on the C3 /i/ and /u/ pages, so there the law, which has no gate, adds the jet's noise; on the phrases it sounded for 0.7 to 11.2 % of each vowel at C3 and 19.5 to 28.0 % at C4. Part of the recordings' floor between the harmonics may be the room.

Pulse shimmer on the 14 graded notes and on the phrases: a per-cycle gain on the glottal pulse, sd 1.13 %, sized from the 1.28 % local shimmer Yoo et al. 2002 report for 65 classical singing students (abstract only; that figure's tracker floor wasn't taken out).
Breath pressure that rises over 150 ms, the centre of a speech range (Fant and Kruckenberg 2005), and is then held.

On the 14 graded notes, a branched airway below the folds, the subglottal_airway row: Weibel's symmetric tree (1963) to 17 generations, with the dimensions Saab et al. print (2021, arXiv:2111.07627, Table 1, column B), from the trachea, 120 mm long and 18 mm across, to generation 17, 1.7 mm by 0.6 mm, each generation's 2^(n-1) tubes in parallel, with Bessel (Zwikker-Kosten) losses in the tract's gas and the card's breath pressure at the far end. It enters the glottis as a causal reflectance on its upstream side, and the fold forces take the pressure at its top. 17 is a convergence count, not a fit. The airway alone took the notes 0.8 to 314.4 c off their pitch; C3-a, C3-i, C3-o, C3-u, C4-a, C4-e, C4-i, C4-o, C4-u, C4-u-rigid, F4-a, F4-e and F4-o were retrimmed to the note for it by the card's own rule (fold stiffness only, pressure held, within 3 c of the written note, no recording), and C3-e stayed within 3 c at the card's own stiffness.
Folds retrimmed per card on the model alone: only the fold stiffnesses move (three on the two-mass cards, four on F4-a), no recording enters, and the tract's passive formants don't change.

One listening page moves the tract within a note (the tract_move row): on C3 the subject's tense /a/ moves to the same subject's tense /i/ between 1.2 and 1.4 s, through 30 frozen shapes, each a log-area average of the two measured charts. It has no recording and no grade. Three limits: the glottal section is held constant, so the /i/ chart's first section takes the /a/ card's area; the mouth radius at the microphone stays the /a/ card's; and the shapes are frozen and crossfaded, coefficient interpolation between linear tracts, with no volume source from moving walls, which a real moving tract has.

One listening page says a word (the fricative_noise, tract_move and rest_gap rows): on C3 the subject's /a/ card says /sa/, with the same subject's measured /s/ as a keyframe, frication noise at its constriction, and the glottis opening and closing over time. It has no recording and no grade, and its stamped voicing test fails: the folds restart at a wider glottis than the human range. Three limits: the times are other speakers' and singers', the glottal gesture between its two measured instants is drawn linear, and the shapes are frozen and crossfaded.
physics_missing: The singer's own tract: these are one man's spoken vowels, and larynx height, pharynx and lip shape differ in singing. The spectrum's tilt follows the subject's vowels, not the singers', and 1-2 kHz is further from the recordings than on the earlier cards on 11 of the 14 pages.

The recordings' noise floor: 9 pages are still cleaner than their recordings, by 0.4 to 13.8 dB, and 5 are less clean, by 0.4 to 9.4 dB, F4-a by the most. Read against each band's own lines, the floor between them sits under the recording's on 9 of the 14 notes at 80 Hz to 1 kHz, 5 at 1-2 kHz, 7 at 2-4 kHz and 8 at 4-8 kHz, and at 8-10 kHz on 7 of the 11 where the recording and the render both have lines there to read against. The constriction noise row and the pulse shimmer are the only sources of energy between the lines on these cards, and what the recordings' floor is hasn't been shown. Between the lines at 300 Hz to 2 kHz, on the lossless clips, the model's falls with distance from the nearest line by 3.5 dB on average at C3, rises with it by 1.4 dB on average at C4 and stays within 1 dB on average at F4, while the recordings' stay within 1 dB at all three; the model's falls at least 3 dB further than the recording's on 4 of the 14 pages. Very roughly a third of the recordings' floor moves with the cycle, what stays isn't shown to be noise, and the printed aspiration level, tried on two pages, moves it by under .1 dB.

Words, consonants and moving tract shapes: fold settings are fixed within a render, each join between vowels in the phrases is a crossfade, and the one page that moves the tract within a note crossfades frozen shapes, each a log-area average of two measured charts. No articulatory model carries that move. Two linear models built on the subject's own MRI were tried between the tense /a/ and the tense /i/, and both missed their stamped predictions. Moved straight in its coefficients, a model of the midsagittal widths keeps both half-formed constrictions, with a single narrowing on 2 of 63 shapes; a model of the tongue contour does the same, on 5 of 63, with 4 shapes whose outline crosses itself. Both rest on 19 of the subject's 22 scans: the /e/, /o/ and "ich" scans could not be placed in a common frame. The width model's laws from midsagittal width to area miss the close vowels on their own: given the tense /u/'s measured widths, they put its second formant at 932 Hz, against 646 Hz from that scan's own cuts. The width model's halfway shape was rendered once on C3, held still, as a dose read: the largest second difference of its pressure at the microphone over 0.5-1.2 s is 1.930 times the /a/ card's, between the log-area halfway shape's 2.174 and the /i/ card's 1.256, and the 0.2 s windows of the two halfway shapes overlap (1.35-2.62 against the log-area shape's 1.63-2.44), so whether the depth of the half-formed constrictions causes the log-area halfway shape's excess over both ends is neither shown nor ruled out.
No print sizes pitch movement under vibrato: the phrases carry the straight-tone sizes there. There are no register changes or formant-tuning gestures.

The singers' tuning and pitch movement: the cards are trimmed to the written note and sit -15.2 to +5.1 cents from equal temperament, while the recordings sit -48.4 to +10.0 cents from it. The period swing over the middle of a clip is 17.7 to 45.6 cents (5-95 %), against 11.5 to 100.6 cents in the recordings.
A sung onset: the pressure rise is a speech value from one male speaker, and no adduction gesture is entered. Attacks read 21 to 81 ms against 22 to 580 ms in the recordings.

Fold tissue: lumped cards, two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes and Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover on F4-a, not continuous layered tissue or a 3-D fold. The damping and collision values are printed typical values of one model each, not measurements of a voice, and one stiffness scale per card stands in for a fold-elongation law; the body-cover report moves pitch with Titze and Story's 2002 muscle rules, which aren't open.

Lungs and airway: the breath pressure is an authored player input on each card, not a measured one. On the 14 graded notes it acts at the far end of a branched airway below the folds, with no lung tissue, chest wall or breathing movement behind it; the phrases keep the ideal port, the pressure straight under the glottis. The airway's walls are a stand-in, the card's vocal-tract wall (Hanna, Smith and Wolfe 2016): supraglottal, measured through the lips with the glottis closed, not subglottal; the per-generation wall data (Habib et al. 1994) is behind a bot check and was not read. With that stand-in the computed airway load misses the measured one: the tree's input impedance peaks at 438, 1192 and 1899 Hz, at 22.99, 22.71 and 13.07 MPa s/m3, against 640, 1400 and 2100 Hz at 2.5 to 5 MPa s/m3 measured by Ishizaka, Matsudaira and Kaneko (1976), about 200 Hz low and 2.6 to 9.2 times too high.
Tract acoustics beyond a single series chain of plane-wave sections: no cross-modes, nasal coupling or side branches.

The piriform fossae as side branches from the DVTD meshes were tested against the measured transfer functions on 8 tracts and failed the stamped gate (trough within 5 % on 0 of 8, band within 2 dB on 0 of 8). A full 3-D FE on the same meshes places the trough on 7 of 8 but stays 2-6 dB high on the 4-8 kHz band. DVTD subject 1's own FE problem, reproduced exactly on s1-02 and s1-17 (trough +0.00 %, bands +0.00 dB), keeps its 4.10 and 4.19 kHz troughs with the whole piriform region cut out: moved 0.00 % and +0.23 %, 9.2 and 12.9 dB shallower. The fossae deepen those troughs but do not set their frequencies, so no side-branch row places them and none is added. The measured and FE troughs were read before this test's rules were written.

The tract above 4 kHz on rounded vowels: on the subject's /o/ and /u/ tracts the cards' one-dimensional chain carries 5.7 to 9.9 dB more at 4-8 kHz than the measured transfer of the same 3-D print, against -0.6 to +3.3 dB on the subject's five unrounded vowels. Under the FE's own laws the same chain sits 1.2 to 7.2 dB over the 3-D FE of the same mesh on the rounded tracts, most of it at 4-5 kHz, and 0.4 to 5.3 dB under it on the unrounded ones, so on three of the four much of the excess is the plane-wave model itself, not the cut. None of the cuts tried (levels of a potential, centreline planes, geodesic shells), and not the paper's lip load, brings any rounded tract within 2 dB at 4-8 kHz.

The wall's detail: it's uniform along the tract, not a measured distribution, and its values are the mean of seven men measured through the lips, not this singer's or the subject's, uncertain by about 35 % on the mass and 50 % on the stiffness; one man's cheek and neck, measured with a shaker on the skin (Ishizaka, French and Flanagan 1975), span 15 to 24 kg/m2 and 8.0e3 to 2.32e4 Pa s/m. The subject's first formants on these cards sit 46 to 72 Hz above the print's measured ones. That gap is the wall, 37 C alveolar air and, by .2 to 1.5 Hz on the renders before the breath, the load of the head and torso at the lips, against a rigid model at room temperature, and the wall hasn't been split from the air.

A singer's torso, the neck, the nose and the lips' shape: the graded notes and the phrases have a rigid spherical head over a rigid spherical torso, the KEMAR snowman of Algazi, Duda and Thompson 2002, and nothing else. KEMAR is a mannequin; the print says a sphere is not a good approximation of the human torso, particularly at low elevations, and it computed the snowman from 0 to 5 kHz. The mouth on the head's horizontal equator facing front, with the microphone at mouth height, is a choice no print makes. On the graded notes and the phrases the lips see the head's own radiation load: the head_load row (the cap on the same sphere, Morse and Ingard 1968 sec. 7.2) on top of the flanged pipe's, which lowered the grade by one row in 135; the torso's change to that load and to the microphone's pressure, below 10 kHz, moved the grade from 134 to 136 rows in 204. Above 10 kHz the pressure is the baffle's. The receiver's resolved band is 8 kHz, so energy above that isn't a prediction.

The breath's onset: a held vowel's first breath is dead-space air, mixed toward room air, before the expired air is alveolar, and the cards hold alveolar air from the first sample. The breath doesn't mix with the room at the lips, and the room itself is a declared state, humid air at 37 C, not a measured one.
Convergence on these cards: no ladder has been run on the tract cards, and the fold clock's earlier ladder used a different tract and law.
